summary: The bill amends the Public Health Service Act to let licensed mental health providers (not just physicians) certify mental health conditions for the World Trade Center Health Program, exclude deceased people from enrollment counts, lengthen deadlines for adding conditions to the covered list, revise the funding formula to grow annual appropriations through 2090 based on prior-year enrollment changes plus a 25% increase option for certain accounts, and require HHS to report long-term budget projections to Congress.

scores.thoughts: The bill directly amends funding formulas in Section 3351 of the Public Health Service Act to increase annual appropriations for the World Trade Center Health Program through fiscal year 2090, including a 7% annual growth factor adjusted by enrollment ratios plus specific 25% increases for FY2026. This constitutes a clear expansion of federal government spending on the program.
The bill contains no provisions related to tax rates, credits, deductions, or revenue collection mechanisms.

The legislation expands access to and administration of a federally funded public health program for 9/11 responders and survivors by broadening provider qualifications for mental health certifications, adjusting enrollment counts, and ensuring sustained program funding. This supports public coverage rather than market-based approaches.
No provisions address firearms, regulations, or Second Amendment issues.
No provisions relate to immigration pathways, border enforcement, or protections for non-citizens.
No provisions address reproductive health services or abortion access.
No provisions affect military budgets, defense programs, or national security spending.
No provisions address environmental regulations, climate policy, or conservation measures.

The bill expands a targeted federal health benefits program for a specific population of responders and survivors, which functions as a form of public safety-net healthcare, though it is not a general welfare program like SNAP or TANF.
No provisions relate to schools, school choice, federal education funding, or privatization.
No provisions address drug enforcement, decriminalization, or substance abuse policy beyond mental health treatment access within the existing program.
No provisions address sentencing, policing, rehabilitation, or criminal justice reform.
No provisions address tariffs, trade agreements, or globalization.
By permanently increasing mandatory-like spending on the WTC Health Program without identified offsets, the bill accepts ongoing deficit financing rather than prioritizing debt reduction.
No provisions address legal protections or rights for LGBTQ+ individuals.
No provisions address foreign assistance, international aid, or related funding.
No provisions address voting access, election integrity, or electoral reforms.
No provisions address technology regulation, data privacy, or digital oversight.
No provisions address union rights, worker protections, or employer flexibility.
No provisions address religious exemptions or civil rights enforcement.

Section 6 substantially revises the WTC Health Program funding formula to provide automatic 7% annual growth plus enrollment adjustments through 2090, plus 25% spending increases in FY2026, directly authorizing higher federal outlays without offsets. This is a core purpose of the bill.

The bill expands and streamlines a federal government health program for 9/11 responders and survivors (mental health provider flexibility, enrollment rules, condition additions, and sustained funding), constituting direct government action to maintain and broaden coverage.
